Het project behoudt niettemin een sterke educatieve dimensie dankzij het uitzicht op de installaties en de haven.

Neem de lift of de buitenpaden om Kopenhagen vanuit een ongebruikelijk perspectief te bekijken. De windmolens, de kanalen, de torens van het centrum en de Øresundbrug verschijnen in één enkel panorama. Het groene glijoppervlak verandert van textuur naargelang het weer; het bootst sneeuw niet exact na, maar maakt gebruik het hele jaar door mogelijk.

CopenHill ligt dicht bij Refshaleøen en kan een bezoek aan Copenhagen Contemporary aanvullen. De sportactiviteiten zijn betalend, terwijl de toegang tot de paden onder specifieke voorwaarden kan vallen. Zelfs zonder te skiën is de plek de moeite waard vanwege de architectuur en het debat dat ze opent over de zichtbaarheid van ons afval.
nl.Centre historique de Køge:
Kirkestræde herbergt enkele van de oudste vakwerkhuizen van Denemarken. Køge werd aan het einde van de 13e eeuw gesticht als koopstad, nabij de monding van de rivier. Het grote, regelmatige marktplein, de haven en de oude straten getuigen van een welvaart die gebouwd was op handel tussen Seeland, de Oostzee en het omliggende platteland.

De stad bezit een opmerkelijk geheel van huizen uit de 16e en 17e eeuw. De zichtbare balken, uitkragende verdiepingen en achtererven laten zien hoe handel, opslag en wonen met elkaar verweven waren. Restauraties hebben onregelmatigheden behouden die al te perfecte reconstructies zouden hebben uitgewist.

Køge is ook verbonden met de heksenprocessen die bekendstaan als Køge Huskors, tussen 1608 en 1615. Beschuldigingen van bezetenheid en toverij leidden tot meerdere executies. Het lokale museum plaatst deze gebeurtenissen in de religieuze en sociale spanningen van die tijd, in plaats van ze te reduceren tot een louter duistere legende.

Bekijk op het plein de royale schaal van de markt en de relatie met de Sint-Nicolaaskerk, waarvan de toren ook dienstdeed als zeevaarwegwijzer. Zoek in Kirkestræde naar de uitgehouwen jaartallen en de verschillen in opvulling tussen de vakwerkconstructies. Elke gevel is een klein document over de beschikbare materialen en de status van de bewoners.

Køge ligt ongeveer veertig kilometer ten zuiden van Kopenhagen en is per trein bereikbaar. De stad is compact genoeg voor een wandeling van enkele uren, maar de moderne haven en het kunstmuseum KØS kunnen het bezoek verlengen. Het is een minder druk alternatief voor Roskilde of Helsingør.

en.Château de Rosenborg et Jardin du Roi:
Rosenborg seems to have been set down in the King’s Garden like a brick casket, bristling with towers and gables. Christian IV had this pleasure residence built starting in 1606, outside the fortifications of the time. Expanded in stages until 1633, the castle adopted the Dutch Renaissance style favored by the sovereign, with red brick, light sandstone, and copper roofs.

The king was not seeking only a backdrop. Rosenborg offered a more intimate refuge than the great official palaces and opened onto a garden designed for leisure, fruit, and flowers. Christian IV died there in 1648. The sovereigns then used the residence less often, which paradoxically helped preserve old interiors and objects.

Since the 19th century, the castle has housed the royal collections. The basement contains the Crown Jewels and the regalia, including the crowns of absolutism. Three life-size silver lions guard the throne; they still appear during castra doloris, the funeral ceremonies for monarchs. Their spectacular brilliance contrasts with the narrow rooms of the house.

The Long Hall, completed in 1624, has a richly decorated ceiling and tapestries recounting Christian V’s victories in the Scanian War. Each room functions like a capsule of a reign: portraits, cabinets, weapons, and furniture show how the monarchy built its image long before modern media.

Outside, notice the iron anchors that reinforce the brick walls and create patterns on the facades. Also look for the differences between the towers: Rosenborg grew through successive additions, and this irregularity gives it its charm. From the bridge, the moat turns the castle into an almost theatrical reflection.

The King’s Garden, open to the public from the 18th century, is today one of the most frequented green spaces in the city center. Picnics, games, and walks surround the former royal retreat. This popular appropriation creates a typically Copenhagen scene: the jewels remain protected underground, while the lawn belongs to everyone.
en.Tour Ronde — Rundetårn:
No grand staircase leads to the top of the Round Tower: a white ramp winds around a hollow core seven and a half times. Christian IV had Rundetårn built between 1637 and 1642 as an observatory for the university. The tower was part of the Trinitatis complex, bringing church, library, and astronomy together in a single scholarly program.

The ramp made it possible to haul instruments, books, and equipment up on carts. According to a famous story, Tsar Peter the Great rode up it on horseback in 1716, while his wife followed in a carriage. The tale perfectly matches the spirit of the place: the ascent is not just a passage, but a physical experience in which the height gained is measured little by little.

At the top, the oldest observatory in Europe still in continuous use remains in operation. After more modern university facilities were installed outside the city center, the tower opened widely to amateur astronomers. Public observations make it possible to see the Moon and the planets when the sky cooperates, reminding us that the building is not only a tourist lookout.

An enigmatic golden inscription runs across the façade. It combines Latin and Hebrew words with a rebus asking God to guide knowledge and justice into the heart of King Christian IV. This blend of scholarship and royal display perfectly suits the sovereign, an indefatigable builder who used architecture to assert his power.

As you climb, look for the small glass floor overlooking the central core. The cavity descends deep below and was long surrounded by unsettling stories. A joke tells of a choirboy who fell in there in the nineteenth century and was found alive; the episode strengthened the local taste for this hidden void at the heart of the tower.

The outer platform offers a circular view of church spires, copper roofs, and inner courtyards. Spot Vor Frue Kirke, Rosenborg, and the spire of Christiansborg. Unlike very high panoramas, this one remains close to the details: chimneys, bicycles, and hidden gardens form a lived-in map of Copenhagen.
en.Cathédrale Notre-Dame — Vor Frue Kirke:
The marble apostles seem to form a silent guard along the white nave. Vor Frue Kirke, Copenhagen’s Lutheran cathedral, owes its present appearance to C. F. Hansen, a leading architect of Danish Neoclassicism. The church was rebuilt after the British bombardment of 1807, which destroyed the previous sanctuary and left a deep mark on the capital.

Yet the religious site is far older. A first church stood here in the 12th century, and several successive buildings fell victim to fires or wars. The present cathedral was consecrated in 1829. Hansen chose calm volumes, pale walls, and a portico of Doric columns, breaking with the Baroque exuberance that had previously dominated.

Bertel Thorvaldsen created the Christ and the twelve apostles that define the interior. Christ opens his arms beneath the inscription “Come unto me,” a gesture that has become one of the most widely reproduced religious images in Denmark. The figures were first modeled in Rome; their luminous white answers the architecture and transforms the nave into a sacred gallery.

The cathedral is also a stage for national history. Danish sovereigns have been crowned or blessed here depending on the period, and major royal weddings have taken place here, notably that of Crown Princess Margrethe and Prince Henrik in 1967. Broadcast ceremonies have given the building a presence far beyond Copenhagen.

Walk slowly down the central axis and notice how the apostles are not fixed to the walls: each has a distinct pose and attribute. The play of light on their draperies brings life to a setting that is almost devoid of color. Outside, the pediment and square tower seem deliberately austere after the theatricality inside.

Vor Frue Kirke tells of the city’s ability to rebuild without erasing the trauma. The bombardment of 1807 belongs to its modern origins, yet the building does not look like a monument to revenge. Hansen and Thorvaldsen preferred monumental serenity, as though the order of the lines were meant to answer the chaos of the flames.
en.Hôtel de Ville et Rådhuspladsen:
The golden dragon watching over the entrance to the City Hall immediately sets the tone: Copenhagen loves to blend civic solemnity with almost fantastical details. The broad Rådhuspladsen, reshaped several times with the arrival of trams, then automobiles, and later the metro, marks the hinge between the old city and the neighborhoods developed beyond the ramparts. Since 1905, the red-brick façade has served as a backdrop for celebrations, demonstrations, and popular New Year’s festivities.

The architect Martin Nyrop designed the building between 1892 and 1905, drawing inspiration from Italian town halls as well as from the Danish brick tradition. He rejected a dutiful historic copy: spires, gables, arches, and wrought iron form a National Romantic ensemble in which craftsmen, sculptors, and painters worked as if on a medieval construction site. The tower rises to about 105 meters and remains one of the best landmarks in the city center.

Behind the façade lies Jens Olsen’s astronomical clock, set in motion in 1955 after decades of calculation and fabrication. Its mechanism indicates not only the time, but also planetary movements, calendars, and astronomical phenomena over immense periods. Olsen, a locksmith who became a clockmaker, did not live to see his work completed: his plans were carried forward by a team of specialists.

The square has known a far noisier life than its present appearance suggests. Tram lines crossed here, newspapers displayed election results here, and residents gathered here to follow the big news. The statue of Andersen, seated at the edge of the traffic, recalls that the writer spent part of his life in the capital and observed its transformations with inexhaustible curiosity.

Approach the main portal and look for the animals, faces, and vegetal motifs scattered through the stone and metal. Then step back to the center of the square: the mass of the City Hall seems lighter thanks to the irregular rhythm of the windows and the outlines of the roofs. The building was designed to be read slowly, detail by detail, rather than as a uniform administrative façade.

Rådhuspladsen remains an excellent barometer of life in Copenhagen. Cyclists speed through toward Vesterbro, pedestrians head to Strøget, and the lights of Tivoli appear just a few steps away. This constant crossroads sums up the capital: a city where municipal power, entertainment, transport, and strolling meet without any real boundary.
en.Jardins de Tivoli:
As soon as you pass through Tivoli’s gates, the noise of the city dissolves into a blend of music, lanterns, shouts, and sweet scents. Opened on 15 August 1843, the pleasure garden was conceived by Georg Carstensen, who persuaded King Christian VIII by claiming that when people are having fun, they do not think about politics. The line was mischievous, but the park became above all a laboratory for modern urban entertainment.

Tivoli has never been content with rides alone. As early as the nineteenth century, it offered theatres, restaurants, concerts, exotic settings, and fireworks. The pantomime theatre, recognizable by its peacock-tail curtain, carries on a tradition inspired by commedia dell’arte. Pierrot, Colombine, and Harlequin still perform wordless stories there, understood by visitors of every language.

The park also preserves one of the oldest wooden roller coasters still in operation, Rutschebanen, inaugurated in 1914. Traditionally, an operator accompanies each train to control its speed manually. This human presence gives the attraction a charm that fully automated systems have made disappear elsewhere. The gardens thus combine new technologies with gestures inherited from another age.

Walt Disney visited Tivoli several times in the 1950s and admired its cleanliness, nighttime atmosphere, and the care devoted to the scenery. It is often said that these visits fed his thinking for Disneyland. Tivoli, for its part, continued to evolve without losing its founding principle: each season transforms the landscape, from spring blooms to the illuminations of Halloween and Christmas.

Look at the small buildings rather than rushing straight to the major attractions. Pagodas, kiosks, Moorish façades, and neoclassical pavilions create an imaginary city inside the real one. In the evening, thousands of lamps trace the outlines of the trees and rooftops; this warm light has been an integral part of the spectacle since the gas era.

Tivoli reveals an essential side of Copenhagen: collective pleasure is treated there with seriousness. Gardeners, musicians, machinists, and restaurateurs create an experience where one can just as easily listen to an orchestra as ride an attraction. The park is neither a frozen museum nor a temporary fair; it is an institution that has been reinventing itself for more than 180 years.
en.Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek:
Beneath the great glass dome, palm trees rise around a fountain, giving the Glyptotek’s winter garden the feel of an unexpected oasis. The museum was founded by the brewer Carl Jacobsen, heir to Carlsberg and a passionate collector. In 1888 he donated part of his works to the city, then financed a building where ancient sculptures, French art, and Danish painting could enter into dialogue far from the industrial bustle.

The first building, designed by Vilhelm Dahlerup, opened in 1897. Hack Kampmann later added a wing inaugurated in 1906, linked by the winter garden. The façades of brick, granite, and marble reveal two architectural temperaments: Dahlerup’s historicist exuberance and Kampmann’s more austere monumentality. A modern extension by Henning Larsen, completed in 1996, completes this ensemble without imitating it.

The word glyptotek literally means a collection of sculptures. The Egyptian, Greek, Etruscan, and Roman galleries make it possible to compare faces, drapery, and ways of representing power. But the museum is just as famous for its 19th-century French paintings and sculptures, with Degas, Rodin, Gauguin, and the Impressionists, as well as for the Danish Golden Age.

Carl Jacobsen saw art as a public good, but he was also a strong-willed man, sometimes in conflict with his father, J. C. Jacobsen. Their rivalry gave rise to two breweries bearing the name Carlsberg. In the museum, this family ambition is transformed into civic generosity: beer wealth finances galleries where the people of Copenhagen can travel from ancient Egypt to Paris without leaving the city.

In the central courtyard, notice the transition between the dark stone, the mosaics, and the light from the roof. The garden is not a mere place of rest: it organizes the route and prepares the eye to move from one era to another. Also look for traces of polychromy on certain ancient sculptures; they remind us that the Greco-Roman world was not as white as 19th-century museums led people to believe.

The Glyptotek works especially well when one accepts unexpected connections. A Roman portrait can seem as psychologically revealing as a modern painting, while a dancer by Degas enters into dialogue with an ancient body. The building itself encourages this curiosity: it accumulates styles, yet brings them together around a simple conviction, that beauty deserves time and a carefully constructed setting.
en.Palais de Christiansborg:
Three branches of power meet under the same roof at Christiansborg: the Parliament, the Prime Minister’s Office, and the Supreme Court. This concentration of institutions is almost unique. Yet the present palace is only the latest chapter in a site occupied since the 12th century, when Bishop Absalon had a fortress built on a small islet opposite the little trading harbor that would become Copenhagen.

The ruins of Absalon’s Castle and the medieval castle that succeeded it are still visible beneath the palace. Above them, two royal residences were devastated by fires, in 1794 and then in 1884. The third Christiansborg, designed by Thorvald Jørgensen, was completed in 1928 in a neo-Baroque style. Its heavy granite façade was meant to convey stability after centuries of destruction and rebuilding.

The monarchy still uses several spaces: the Royal Reception Rooms, the stables, and the chapel. The queen — and then the king — receives official guests there, holds banquets, and receives ambassadors. The modern tapestries by Bjørn Nørgaard, presented in 2000, tell a thousand years of Danish history with a profusion of figures, symbols, and contemporary allusions.

Christiansborg Tower, 106 meters high, rises slightly above City Hall Tower. It has become a popular viewpoint, but for a long time its silhouette was criticized for its bulk. A joke says that the architect added crowns at the top to correct the impression of a tower that was too flat. Whether true or not, the anecdote reflects Copenhageners’ attention to their skyline.

In the square, look for the equestrian statue of Frederik VII, the king who signed the Constitution of 1849 and brought absolutism to an end. Then examine the dark stones of the base: they anchor the building like a fortress, while the regular windows announce an administrative palace. Nearby, the canals recall that Slotsholmen was first and foremost a strategic island.

Christiansborg sums up the passage from personal power to constitutional power. Kings lived here, the palaces burned, members of parliament debate here today, and royal ceremonies continue. The monument therefore tells not a clear-cut break, but a constant negotiation between tradition, democracy, and national representation.
en.Højbro Plads, statue d’Absalon et Gammel:
Absalon’s horse rears up facing the canal, as if the warrior bishop were still keeping watch over the harbor he helped fortify around 1167. The statue, unveiled in 1902 and sculpted by Vilhelm Bissen, combines two images of the figure: the man of the Church wears the mitre, while the military founder holds an axe. Beneath its hooves, the pedestal evokes herring barrels, an essential wealth of medieval trade.

Højbro Plads did not exist in this form before the great fire of 1795. The authorities took advantage of the destruction to create a more open square, improve circulation, and reduce the risk of fire spreading. The houses surrounding it illustrate Copenhagen’s neoclassical reconstruction: regular façades, chamfered corners, and restrained ornament replaced part of the tighter fabric of the old city.

On the other side of the bridge, Gammel Strand was for centuries the domain of the fishwives. They sold the catch brought in from the coast, notably by the women of Skovshoved, recognizable by their traditional clothing. Their voices, baskets, and the smell of fish formed an everyday backdrop far removed from the elegant promenade of today. A contemporary sculpture recalls this female presence.

The canal follows the former shoreline. Before the land reclamation, the water came much closer to the urban core. Trading boats, markets, and bridges explain the very name København, the “merchant’s harbor.” From Højbro, the relationship between the city and the water appears more clearly than on the great inland squares.

Stand near the statue and look toward Christiansborg: symbolically, Absalon turns his back on the city to defend the maritime approach. Also notice the decoration on the pedestal and the difference between the façades from the early 19th century and the older buildings on Slotsholmen. This small space functions as a lesson in urban planning born of a fire.

Today, terraces, the Christmas market, and passersby have replaced the fish trade, but the square remains a crossroads. From here, one can move from Strøget to the institutions of Christiansborg, from the shopping district to the old shoreline. The history of Absalon, the fires, and the fishwives is concentrated here in just a few dozen meters.
en.Kongens Nytorv:
At the center of Kongens Nytorv, Christian V presides over the traffic on a rearing horse, surrounded by trimmed trees and façades that tell three centuries of urban prestige. The king had the “New King’s Square” laid out from 1670 onward, beyond the old eastern rampart. It was meant to serve as a monumental salon for the expanded city and to connect the commercial heart with the aristocratic district then under construction.

The equestrian statue, created by Abraham-César Lamoureux and unveiled in 1688, was the first royal equestrian statue in Scandinavia. The original lead figure suffered under its own weight and had to be reinforced; a bronze copy replaced it in 1946. Around the pedestal, allegorical figures stage strength, honor, prudence, and piety, the qualities expected of an absolute ruler.

The buildings form a panorama of Copenhagen society. The Royal Theatre recalls the importance of ballet and theater, the Hotel d’Angleterre that of elegant travel, while Charlottenborg Palace houses the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts. Magasin du Nord represents the rise of department stores in the 19th century. The square is therefore less uniform than it appears: each façade belongs to a different era and a different function.

For decades, construction of the metro turned the place into a building site. The opening of the Cityringen station in 2019 restored a vast pedestrian area and strengthened its role as a crossroads. Beneath the paving stones, archaeologists found traces of the fortifications and the city’s growth, proof that even a “new” square rests on older boundaries.

Walk slowly around the statue and look for changes in perspective. Toward Nyhavn, the view slips between the colorful façades; toward Bredgade, the axis leads to Frederiksstaden and Amalienborg. Also observe the trees arranged in an ellipse, heirs to an urban garden where high society once came to be seen.

Kongens Nytorv still preserves this function as a public stage. Theater premieres, Christmas lights, departures for Nyhavn, and meetings by the metro all overlap here. The square created to glorify an absolute king has become a space where tourists, office workers, artists, and cyclists cross paths on equal terms of movement.
en.Nyhavn:
The yellow, red, and orange façades of Nyhavn are reflected in a canal where historic sailing ships and excursion boats share the water. The “new harbor” was dug between 1671 and 1673 by soldiers and Swedish prisoners of war. It allowed merchant ships to reach Kongens Nytorv, bringing cargoes, warehouses, and taverns closer to the center.

The oldest house, at number 9, dates from 1681 and has retained modest proportions. Other buildings were expanded in step with maritime trade. The current colors do not all correspond to an original palette carefully preserved; they are the result of successive restorations that transformed a rough sailors’ district into an emblematic image of the capital.

Hans Christian Andersen lived at several addresses along the canal, notably numbers 20, 67, and 18. There he wrote or finished some of his tales, observing from his windows a world of captains, servants, travelers, and poor people. This closeness to departures and returns suits an author whose characters often leave home to discover a wider world.

Nyhavn long had a rowdy reputation. Inns, tattoo artists, and brothels accompanied the life of the crews. After the Second World War, the decline of short-sea shipping threatened to leave the canal abandoned. The creation of a harbor for historic boats and the gradual pedestrianization gave the district back its heritage value, long before it became one of the most photographed places in Denmark.

Look at the moored hulls on the sunny side and spot the plaques describing certain ships. On the façades, compare the irregular widths of the plots and the pulleys still visible near the gables: they were used to hoist goods up to the attics. The colorful setting thus still bears traces of its working past.

The best way to understand Nyhavn is to imagine the noise of long ago: ropes, barrels, clogs, and sailors’ calls rather than glasses on the terraces. The canal has become peaceful, but its tourist success rests precisely on this former gateway between Copenhagen and the world.
en.Palais d’Amalienborg:
Four nearly identical palaces frame an octagonal square where the royal guard crosses the cobblestones at midday. Amalienborg was not designed as a single residence: the houses were built in the 1750s for four noble families in the heart of Frederiksstaden, the district created to celebrate the tricentennial of the House of Oldenburg.

Nicolai Eigtved directed the ensemble in a restrained Danish Rococo style. The pale stone façades, copper roofs, and corner pavilions create a remarkable symmetry, yet each palace has its own details and history. After the fire at Christiansborg in 1794, the royal family bought the buildings and moved in. A temporary solution thus became Copenhagen’s main monarchical home.

At the center stands Frederik V on horseback, a work by the French sculptor Jacques Saly. Unveiled in 1771, the statue took more than twenty years to complete and cost a considerable sum to the Danish Asiatic Company, which financed it. The horse moves forward calmly rather than at a gallop: the intended image is one of controlled authority.

The changing of the guard departs from Rosenborg and usually arrives at midday when the sovereign is staying at the palace. The uniform, the music, and the route through the streets turn a security necessity into a public ritual. The flags raised on the roofs let those who know read the royal presence and identify which house is occupied.

Stand near the statue and slowly turn around. Look for the differences in gateways, balconies, and coats of arms between the four façades. Then look along the axis toward the harbor: the Opera House now closes the perspective, while the dome of the Marble Church rises behind you.

Amalienborg offers a monarchy that is visible yet protected. The private apartments remain behind the windows, while the square stays open to traffic and visitors. This controlled proximity fits well with the contemporary image of the Danish monarchy: ancient, ceremonial, yet woven into the everyday fabric of the capital.
en.Église de Marbre — Marmorkirken:
The green dome of Marmorkirken seems to close off the axis of Amalienborg like the full stop at the end of a royal composition. Frederik V laid the first stone in 1749 as part of Frederiksstaden. Nicolai Eigtved envisioned a monumental church in Norwegian marble, but costs soared, the work stopped in 1770, and the ruin remained open for more than a century.

The industrialist Carl Frederik Tietgen eventually bought the site and financed its completion. Architect Ferdinand Meldahl scaled back the project, used a great deal of Danish limestone rather than the marble originally planned, and took inspiration from St. Peter’s in Rome. The church was consecrated in 1894, one hundred and forty-five years after construction began.

The dome, about thirty-one meters wide, is the largest in Scandinavia. It rests on twelve columns and overlooks a circular interior where light glides across marble, stucco, and paintings. Around the exterior, statues represent figures from the history of the Church, creating a stone procession above the street.

The very long abandonment of the site gave rise to stories. Generations of Copenhageners knew the building as a romantic shell, overrun with vegetation and used for games. When Tietgen took over the project, he was granted the right to build around the church in return, making the operation as much a real-estate venture as a philanthropic gesture.

Approach the drum and count the visible columns before looking up at the copper dome. From Amalienborg, notice how the dome seems perfectly centered, even though the church and the square belong to very different histories of construction. Inside, the eye is drawn upward rather than along a long nave.

Marmorkirken is a monument to urban patience. It bears the name of a material used less extensively than planned, was completed in a style different from the original design, and owes its survival to a nineteenth-century industrialist. Its present harmony thus conceals a century of debt, abandonment, and compromise.
en.Børsen et sa flèche aux dragons:
Four dragon tails coil together to form the most distinctive spire in Copenhagen. Børsen, the former stock exchange, was commissioned by Christian IV and built from 1619 to 1640 to give Danish commerce a setting worthy of royal ambitions. At the time, the building stood in a strategic location between the city and the new maritime district of Christianshavn.

The brothers Lorenz and Hans van Steenwinckel took part in the project in a Dutch Renaissance style. The long brick façade, the sandstone gables, and the copper roof create an instantly recognizable silhouette. The spire was added in 1625; its dragons traditionally symbolized protection against enemies and fire, a promise that became painfully ironic in April 2024.

On 16 April 2024, a fire broke out during restoration work. Images of the spire collapsing circled the world. Employees, firefighters, and passersby спасued paintings and furniture by carrying them out of the building. No lives were lost, but a major part of the roof and the interiors disappeared. The reconstruction underway aims to restore the historic silhouette while improving safety.

Before this fire, Børsen had already changed function. Merchants once rented spaces there in a large hall where goods, insurance, and capital were negotiated. The building later became the headquarters of the Danish Chamber of Commerce. Its length is a reminder that this was not a compact palace, but a true covered commercial street.

Notice the alternating gables and the almost musical rhythm of the windows. Even when scaffolding hides part of the monument, the relationship between the red brick, the light sandstone, and the copper remains clear. The base follows the canal, recalling that goods arrived as close as possible by boat.

Børsen is now as much a site of memory as a construction site of stone. The capital must decide how to rebuild a symbol of which part of the authentic fabric vanished before the eyes of millions. The future spire will not be the one from 1625, but it will bear the mark of a collective effort comparable to the one that saved the artworks amid the flames.
en.Diamant Noir — Bibliothèque royale:
A black, gleaming block seems to slide toward the harbor, split by a large glass fissure. The Black Diamond, an extension of the Royal Library, was inaugurated in 1999. The architects at Schmidt Hammer Lassen chose granite from Zimbabwe polished like a mirror; depending on the light, the façade turns black, blue, or silvery and reflects the clouds, the water, and the buildings of Christianshavn.

The modern building enters into dialogue with the old library from 1906, located behind it. Walkways span the street and connect two eras of the institution. The Royal Library itself dates back to 1648, when Frederik III assembled a collection intended for the monarchy. Today it is the national and university library, guardian of manuscripts, maps, photographs, scores, and Danish publications.

The vast interior atrium opens onto the canal like a shaft of light. Balconies ripple along the walls, while escalators carry readers and visitors between levels. The architecture does not seek to project the silent image of a closed strongbox: concerts, exhibitions, a café, and an auditorium make the building a cultural venue threaded through by the city.

The library also bears the memory of a spectacular theft. Between the 1960s and 1970s, an employee stole thousands of valuable volumes, including rare editions. The case was not solved until 2003, after an attempt to sell a book at Christie’s. This story of a hidden collection seems almost written for a detective novel.

From the quay, look for the irregular vertical line of the glass façade: it breaks the symmetry and reveals the atrium. Then notice the lean of the two granite masses, slightly tilted toward the canal. The effect is deliberately dynamic, as if the building were a ship moored at Slotsholmen.

The Black Diamond shows how Copenhagen reclaimed its waterfront at the end of the twentieth century. A scholarly institution, once turned inward toward its book stacks, now opens itself to the harbor landscape. Here you can read, listen to a concert, or simply follow the reflections on the granite: three different ways of inhabiting a library.
en.La Petite Sirène:
The Little Mermaid is smaller than many visitors imagine: a young bronze woman seated just above the water, exposed to the wind and to onlookers. Carl Jacobsen, heir to Carlsberg, commissioned the sculpture after seeing a ballet inspired by Hans Christian Andersen’s fairy tale. Edvard Eriksen created it, and the work was unveiled on August 23, 1913.

The dancer Ellen Price inspired the face, but she refused to pose nude. The body was therefore modeled after Eline Eriksen, the sculptor’s wife. This division between two models curiously reflects the character in the tale, who is also divided between two worlds, that of the sea and that of humans.

Andersen’s story, published in 1837, is much darker than some modern adaptations. The mermaid accepts pain and loses her voice to obtain a soul and the love of a prince, without receiving the expected happy ending. The statue avoids any spectacular narrative setting: its withdrawn posture and gaze toward land suggest waiting rather than triumph.

The work has suffered numerous acts of vandalism. It was beheaded in 1964 and in 1998, lost an arm in 1984, was painted, and was symbolically moved several times. Each restoration has strengthened its fame. The original statue traveled exceptionally to Shanghai in 2010 for the World Expo, leaving a video installation in its place.

Look at the point of contact between the legs and the tail: Eriksen chose an unfinished, almost anatomical transformation rather than a fantastical fish. Also observe the surface of the bronze, marked by salt and restorations. The rock and the horizon matter as much as the figure; without them, its hesitation would lose some of its force.

This stop makes a fitting end to a long journey through Copenhagen. A monument funded by beer, inspired by a ballet, and drawn from a melancholic fairy tale has become a global emblem. Its modesty is part of its message: the capital is not defined only by massive palaces; it also knows how to entrust its image to a silent silhouette at the edge of the Øresund.
en.Kastellet:
Seen from above, Kastellet draws a perfect star; at ground level, it appears more like a small military town of red houses, moats, and grassy paths. Christian IV launched the first fortification in 1626, but the present complex owes much to Frederik III and the engineer Henrik Rüse, who reshaped it after the Swedish siege of 1658–1660.

The five bastions bear royal names: of the King, the Queen, the Count, the Princess, and the Prince. They made it possible to fire crosswise along the ramparts, eliminating the blind spots of older medieval enclosures. The moats and glacis created a defensive depth that the modern walkway makes seem almost bucolic.

The citadel remains an active military site, occupied by Danish Defence services, but a large part is open to the public. The orderly buildings, the church, the former prison, and the commandant’s house show how a garrison lived independently. The windmill, rebuilt in 1847, could supply flour if the fortress were isolated during a siege.

Kastellet played a role during the German occupation from 1940 to 1945. German forces used it as a headquarters and prison. Today, several nearby memorials, including the Allied soldiers’ memorial and the Resistance Museum, place the citadel within a broader military memory than that of its 17th-century bastions alone.

Climb onto the rampart path and follow the angles rather than cutting through the center. At each point, the view changes abruptly: harbor, rooftops, St. Alban’s Church, and rows of trees appear and then disappear. Spot the white windmill and the sentries at the gates, a discreet reminder that the park is not entirely decommissioned.

Kastellet’s success lies in this dual life. It is a remarkably well-preserved fortification, but also a place for jogging, strolling, and working. The lines designed for war now serve to slow the pace and offer unexpected views of Copenhagen.
en.Fontaine de Gefion et église Saint-Alban:
Four oxen plough the water with an almost furious energy as the goddess Gefion drives them forward. The fountain was sculpted by Anders Bundgaard and inaugurated in 1908, after a project launched for the fiftieth anniversary of the Carlsberg brewery. It illustrates a Nordic legend explaining the birth of the island of Zealand, on which Copenhagen stands.

According to the tale, the king of Sweden promised Gefion as much land as she could plough in one night. The goddess turned her four sons into oxen, tore away a huge piece of territory, and hurled it into the sea. The void was said to become Lake Mälaren, whose shape vaguely resembles that of Zealand. The sculpture transforms this mythical geography into a muscular scene.

Next to it stands Saint Alban's, an Anglican church consecrated in 1887. Its neo-Gothic style, pale stone, and slender spire contrast with the lively mass of the fountain. The Prince of Wales, later Edward VII, took part in the laying of the foundation stone, recalling the dynastic ties between the British and Danish courts.

The fountain was installed near Kastellet after several hesitations over its location. Its hydraulic mechanism and constant contact with water have required numerous restorations. When it is working at full power, the jets reinforce the impression that the animals are truly tearing up the ground; when it is dry, the anatomical work of the bronze is easier to see.

Look beneath the hooves for the rocks, plants, and secondary animals. Bundgaard did not limit himself to the main figures: he built an entire landscape around the myth. Then compare the site's two verticals, the light spire of Saint Alban's and the group of Gefion pushing horizontally toward the basin.

This corner of the park brings together three stories: a creation legend, a church intended for the British community, and the old defenses of Kastellet. The walk feels peaceful, but it layers mythology, diplomacy, and military urban planning in just a few steps.
en.Opéra de Copenhague:
On the other side of the Royal Basin, the Opera House roof projects like a vast visor above a glass façade. The building was gifted to the Danish state by the A. P. Møller Foundation and inaugurated in January 2005. Its location on Holmen extends a spectacular axis: the Marble Church, Amalienborg, the Royal Square, and the Opera House face one another across the water.

Henning Larsen led the project, but relations with the patron Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller were difficult. The architect publicly criticized certain changes, especially the metal elements of the façade, and distanced himself from the final result. This tension is a reminder that a major cultural venue is also the product of financial, political, and personal decisions.

The main hall seats about 1,700 spectators. Its horseshoe-shaped auditorium is inspired by the European tradition, while the foyer displays contemporary works and light fixtures designed by Olafur Eliasson. Maple wood, gold leaf, and curved surfaces create a warmer atmosphere than the outer shell suggests.

Holmen was once a closed naval area. Shipyards, warehouses, and barracks occupied these artificial islands. The construction of the Opera House contributed to their cultural and residential redevelopment, alongside the School of Architecture and the nearby workshops. Today, the public crosses a former military landscape to attend Mozart, Wagner, or a Bournonville ballet.

From the opposite quay, check the alignment with Amalienborg and the dome of Marmorkirken. As you move closer, notice how the roof seems almost to float, supported by a transparent façade. The luminous sculpture in the foyer is visible from outside at night, turning the building into a lantern on the harbor.

The Opera House still divides architecture lovers, which is no flaw for a contemporary landmark. Some admire its power and luxury, while others regret the heaviness of the roof. This ongoing debate gives it urban life: it does not merely host performances, it also sparks them before the curtain even rises.
en.Église de Notre-Sauveur — Vor Frelsers K:
A gilded exterior staircase winds around the spire of Vor Frelsers Kirke and narrows until it disappears beneath the statue of Christ. The church was built between 1682 and 1696 to plans by Lambert van Haven for the new district of Christianshavn. Its present tower, designed by Lauritz de Thurah, was completed in 1752 and became one of the city’s boldest landmarks.

The climb has about four hundred steps, the last of which run outside. The counterclockwise direction often intrigues visitors. A legend claims that the architect threw himself from the top after discovering a rotational error; it is false, since de Thurah died peacefully seven years later. But the legend matches the vertigo the spire inspires.

Inside, Nicodemus Tessin’s Baroque altar stages angels around Christ in the Garden of Gethsemane. The monumental organ, supported by elephants, dates from the late 17th century. These decorations recall that Christianshavn was not only a practical district of canals and warehouses: the monarchy wanted to give it a spectacular church.

The carillon has forty-eight bells and rings regularly above the rooftops. The sound carries over the canals and out to the harbor, once much quieter. For sailors, the spire served as a visual landmark; for residents, the bells marked the day long before digital watches.

From the square, look for the gold figures on the dial and the copper details. If the climb is open and the wind allows it, watch the landscape gradually change: first the courtyards of Christianshavn appear, then the harbor basins, and finally the entire capital. The last section is narrow; you have to let other visitors pass patiently.

Vor Frelsers Kirke combines highly calculated architecture with an almost adventurous feeling. Baroque here seeks to set the body in motion: lifting one’s head, circling the tower, counting the steps, and facing the void. Few churches make the distance between the street and the sky feel so immediate.
en.Freetown Christiania:
The motto “You are now entering the European Union” appears on the back of Christiania’s famous gate: it is read when leaving the neighborhood, as a joke about its special status. The community was born in 1971 when residents occupied the former Bådsmandsstræde barracks, abandoned by the army. Squats, workshops, and collective experiments quickly transformed the buildings and grounds.

Christiania defines itself as a self-governing society where decisions are traditionally made by consensus. The neighborhood has developed its own rules, its services, its music venues, and a makeshift architecture, often built with reclaimed materials. This freedom has never meant the absence of conflict: relations with the state, land status, security, and the cannabis market have led to decades of negotiations.

Pusher Street became the site’s most controversial symbol. Open cannabis trade attracted tourists, gangs, and police interventions, in contradiction with the community project of many residents. After several violent episodes, the residents took part in 2024 in the physical dismantling of the street as it had functioned, marking a desire to redefine the neighborhood’s image.

Christiania’s appeal goes far beyond this street. Concert halls such as Loppen, workshops, vegetarian restaurants, gardens, and experimental houses form a unique landscape. Some buildings by the water seem straight out of an ecological fairy tale. The walls covered in murals change regularly, which makes any visual description quickly outdated.

Respect the signs and people’s privacy. Photography may be restricted in some areas, and the houses are homes, not sets. Instead, look for the details of reuse: mismatched windows, reclaimed wood, mosaics, and sculptures made from ordinary objects. The neighborhood is read through these improvised solutions more than through a central monument.

Christiania remains an unfinished urban experiment. It has survived efforts to normalize it, collectively bought part of its land, and continues to debate its future. This blend of freedom, contradiction, and responsibility explains why the place fascinates as much as it unsettles.
en.Palais et jardins de Frederiksberg:
At the top of Frederiksberg Hill, the yellow palace dominates lawns that slope down toward winding canals. Frederik IV began the residence in 1699 after a trip to Italy; the building was enlarged in the early 18th century and served as a summer home for the royal family until the mid-19th century. Its elevated position still offers one of the most elegant views in western Copenhagen.

The garden evolved from a formal Baroque design into a romantic landscaped park around 1800. Curving paths, bridges, islands, and groves replaced some of the rigid axes. A Chinese pavilion from 1803 recalls Europe’s taste for distant architectures, while a temple to Apollo and small follies invited strollers to change mood in just a few minutes.

A surprising anecdote links the park to the neighboring zoo: from certain points, you can see the elephants in their enclosure, designed by Norman Foster. A landscaped viewing window has been created so that visitors can watch them for free. The presence of these animals at the end of a royal lawn creates a distinctly Copenhagen collision of heritage, leisure, and everyday life.

The palace now houses the Royal Danish Military Academy. Interior visits are therefore limited and arranged on specific dates, but the exterior and gardens are enough to tell the story of the site. Look at the layout of the wings, the dark roofs, and the way the main façade takes advantage of the terrain rather than a large enclosed courtyard.

Take the time to follow the canals to the Chinese pavilion, then head back up toward Søndermarken. Runners, families, and students have turned this royal estate into a large urban park. Its charm lies less in a single monument than in the succession of views arranged like scenes in a green theater.
en.Cisternerne sous Søndermarken:
Beneath the lawn of Søndermarken stretches a world of damp columns, echoes, and twilight. The cisterns were built in the 19th century to improve Copenhagen’s water supply after epidemics and fires had revealed the fragility of the old wells. They could hold millions of liters, protected from the light in a vast vaulted reservoir.

The network stopped serving drinking water in 1933 and was eventually emptied. For decades, this underground space remained almost forgotten. Its stable temperature, seepage, and exceptional acoustics, however, made it an ideal venue for contemporary art. Cisternerne opened as an exhibition space and now belongs to the Frederiksberg museums.

Each artist must work with a building that refuses neutrality. Water drips, the floor can be uneven, and the columns disappear into darkness. Some installations use light, sound, or mist to transform the reservoir; others let the architecture take center stage. The visit feels more like an exploration than a traditional gallery route.

At the entrance, look at the two glass pavilions in the park: they lead down to infrastructure that is invisible from the outside. Once underground, let your eyes adjust before moving on. The reflections in the puddles and the echo of footsteps on the vaults create a depth that is hard to measure.

The site is cool even in summer and is not always suitable for strollers or for people sensitive to humidity. It is worth checking the current exhibition, as the experience changes radically each year. Cisternerne is a reminder that a city can turn an abandoned technical facility into an artistic adventure without erasing its original materiality.
en.Porte des Éléphants et quartier Carlsber:
Four granite elephants support a tower in the heart of the former Carlsberg brewery. Carl Jacobsen had the Elephant Gate built in 1901 as the monumental entrance to his new brewery. Each animal bears the initial of one of his children; the symbol also came from his interest in antiquity and from the idea of stable strength supporting industry.

Carlsberg was born in 1847 through the initiative of J. C. Jacobsen, who gave the brewery the name of his son Carl, combined with the Danish word for hill, “bjerg.” Father and son quarrelled fiercely and for a time ran two neighboring companies, Old Carlsberg and New Carlsberg. Their rivalry produced laboratories, spectacular buildings, and lasting cultural philanthropy.

The Carlsberg Laboratory helped isolate a pure yeast in 1883 thanks to the scientist Emil Christian Hansen. This breakthrough made fermentation more regular and was shared with other brewers. The district therefore tells as much of the story of microbiology as it does of beer. Chimneys, silos, and former brewhouses now stand alongside housing, offices, and cultural spaces.

Move close to the elephants to see the texture of the Bornholm granite, the sculpted coverings, and the decorative signs, now controversial, drawn from the symbolic vocabulary of the time. Passing beneath the tower creates an almost ceremonial feeling, as if the factory had sought to give itself the dignity of a palace.

The transformation of Carlsberg Byen is not yet complete: contemporary towers and new streets surround the listed buildings. A walk here lets you follow the contrast between industrial heritage and dense urban planning. The best stop is the one where the elephants, impassive, seem to judge more than a century of change.
en.Cimetière Assistens:
Assistens sometimes feels more like a romantic park than a cemetery. Opened in 1760 outside the ramparts, it was meant to relieve the small parish cemeteries in the city center. The first burials were mostly of modest residents, but the elite later embraced the place, drawn by its open space and by the possibility of creating landscaped tombs.

Hans Christian Andersen, Søren Kierkegaard, the physicist Niels Bohr, and many figures from the arts, politics, and everyday life rest here. Their graves attract visitors, but a stroll also reveals thousands of lesser-known lives. The Danish, German, and Hebrew inscriptions bear witness to a diverse capital over more than two centuries.

In the 19th century, families were already coming here to walk among the graves. That habit continues: residents of Nørrebro read, talk, or cross the cemetery by bicycle along the authorized paths. This coexistence calls for respect, especially during ceremonies. The site is not an abandoned backdrop; it remains a place of burial and living memory.

Look for Andersen’s simple grave, enclosed by a low fence, then Kierkegaard’s in the family plot. Notice the styles of the monuments: neoclassical urns, romantic angels, modernist stelae, and nearly anonymous stones make up a history of how the people of Copenhagen have represented death.

The tall trees give the place a different atmosphere in every season. In spring, the greenery softens the lines; in autumn, the stones reappear beneath the leaves. A map is useful for finding notable figures, but you should also allow yourself to get lost in the paths: Assistens is understood through its silences as much as through its famous names.
en.Superkilen:
A black bull from Spain, benches from Baghdad, and equipment borrowed from dozens of countries make up Superkilen. The park was inaugurated in 2012 in the multicultural district of Nørrebro. BIG, Topotek1, and the artistic collective Superflex worked with local residents to choose objects evoking their origins, their journeys, or their memories.

The space is organized into three sections: the Red Square, dedicated to sports and cultural activities, the more mineral Black Market, and the Green Park. Color is not just a graphic decoration; it helps make sense of how the space is used and gives a strong identity to an urban strip once fragmented by traffic and leftover plots.

Each object has a geographical story, sometimes marked by a plaque. Yet the project avoids turning cultures into static folkloric displays: the benches are genuinely used, the playgrounds are occupied, and teenagers make the surfaces their own. Signs from all over the world become everyday Danish street furniture.

The famous striped surface of the Black Market distorts perception and produces almost abstract photographs. Notice how the lines curve around the trees and furniture, then look for the inscriptions identifying where the objects come from. Diversity is written into the details rather than summed up by a central monument.

Superkilen is very lively and sometimes noisy. A daytime visit lets you observe families, skateboarders, and cyclists; in the evening, the atmosphere changes. The park does not claim to solve all of Nørrebro’s social challenges, but it shows how a public project can begin with residents’ stories rather than a catalog of standard furniture.
en.Église de Grundtvig:
The façade of Grundtvig's Church rises like a gigantic organ above the small yellow houses of Bispebjerg. Peder Vilhelm Jensen-Klint won the competition in 1913 for a monument dedicated to the pastor, poet, and thinker N. F. S. Grundtvig. The foundation stone was laid in 1921; after the architect's death, his son Kaare Klint completed the church in 1940.

About six million yellow bricks were used. Jensen-Klint combined the stepped gable of Danish rural churches with Gothic verticality and an almost modern abstraction. No luxurious cladding conceals the material: walls, pillars, and vaults draw their strength from the precise repetition of brick.

Grundtvig championed a lively popular education and inspired the folk high school movement. The church does not tell his biography through an abundance of statues; instead, it translates his ideas into a collective architecture, built with an ordinary material raised to monumental dignity.

Enter if the schedule allows, and let your gaze follow the pillars up to the vaults. The cool light accentuates the warm color of the bricks, and the furnishings designed by Kaare Klint extend the austerity of the whole. Outside, compare the western tower with the façades of the neighboring housing, designed in the same garden-city spirit.

The district lies away from the classic tourist routes, which makes the arrival all the more impressive. The church suddenly appears at the end of a quiet street. It is one of the finest examples of brick Expressionism in Europe and proves that modern Danish architecture did not begin with glass and steel, but with a radical reinterpretation of local traditions.
en.Den Blå Planet — Aquarium national:
Seen from the sky, Den Blå Planet looks like a whirlpool set on the edge of the Øresund. The national aquarium opened in Kastrup in 2013, replacing the former facility in Charlottenlund. The 3XN studio arranged the wings around a spiral center so that visitors are drawn into different marine worlds without losing their bearings.

The complex features tropical waters, reefs, large ocean tanks, and Nordic habitats. A transparent tunnel lets visitors watch sharks and rays pass overhead. The exhibitions also focus on ecosystems, reproduction, and the threats posed by pollution rather than on a simple accumulation of spectacular animals.

Its location near the airport and the sea is strategic. Water from the Øresund can be used for certain systems, while the building becomes a landmark for travelers arriving on Amager. Its pale metal skin changes with the sky, evoking scales without copying the shape of a fish.

Outside, notice the curves converging toward the entrance; inside, spot the technical areas visible behind the aquariums. Feeding, filtering, and maintaining thousands of organisms requires infrastructure as complex as the scenography. Children enjoy the touch pools, but adults will benefit from reading the panels devoted to local species.

Prices and opening hours vary by season, and buying online can be advantageous. The Kastrup metro station makes the trip easy from the city center. A full visit takes several hours: Den Blå Planet is not just a quick detour before a flight, but a destination in its own right for science and family outings.
en.Vieille ville de Dragør:
The yellow façades of Dragør seem to have been arranged around the old harbor by a decorator in love with hollyhocks. This maritime town on Amager prospered from the Middle Ages onward thanks to herring fishing and then coastal trade. In the 18th and 19th centuries, its captains and shipowners had low houses built, set close together to resist the wind and painted in warm tones that brighten gray days.

The layout of the narrow streets tells the story of a community turned toward the sea. The narrow gables, tiled roofs, and small sheltered gardens formed a practical fabric rather than a picturesque design. When sail navigation declined, Dragør escaped drastic transformations; this relative economic stagnation paradoxically helped preserve its character.

During the German occupation, the port played an essential role in the rescue of Danish Jews. In October 1943, fishermen and residents secretly transported families to Sweden, visible on the other side of the Øresund. The local museum and several plaques recall this episode, when working boats became instruments of survival.

Walk slowly along Strandstræde and look for the mirrors fixed to the windows: these devices once made it possible to observe the street without leaving one’s armchair. At the harbor, compare the wooden sheds, the traditional boats, and the modern facilities. The most accurate understanding comes from the contrast between a preserved village and a still-living municipality.

Dragør is easy to reach from Copenhagen, but it deserves more than a quick photograph. The cafés and quays are lively in summer; early in the morning or out of season, the silence brings out the creaking of the masts and the smell of seaweed. This excursion offers the most intimate version of the capital’s maritime history.
en.Jægersborg Dyrehave:
Hundreds of deer roam freely beneath old oaks in Jægersborg Dyrehave, a former royal hunting reserve transformed into a public landscape. Christian V had the estate enclosed in the 1670s to practice par force hunting, a spectacular discipline in which riders and hounds pursued the game according to court ceremonial.

The long avenues radiate from the Hermitage, a hunting pavilion completed in 1736 by Lauritz de Thurah. This geometric plan made it possible to track the animals and organize the hunt, but today it creates striking perspectives through the forest. The site belongs to the Par force hunting landscape of North Zealand, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2015.

The population includes fallow deer, red deer, and sika deer. It is important to keep your distance, especially during the autumn rut and the calving season. The animals are not domesticated despite their apparent calm. Their grazing maintains clearings and supports a mosaic of habitats that is rare near a major capital.

Near Klampenborg, the red gates mark the historic entrances. Follow an avenue to the Hermitage, then leave it to observe the gnarled trees, the terrain, and the herds of deer. Hollow trunks shelter insects, fungi, and birds; the natural heritage is as important as the royal setting.

Dyrehaven changes dramatically with the seasons: anemones in spring, deep shadows in summer, the roar of deer in autumn, and bare silhouettes in winter. Cyclists, riders, and walkers share the estate. Half a day is enough to combine forest, architecture, and, if you continue toward the coast, the beaches of Klampenborg.
en.Bellevue et Bellavista:
The white balconies of Bellavista are oriented like theater seats toward the Øresund. Arne Jacobsen designed this residential complex in the early 1930s, at the same time as Bellevue Beach and several neighboring facilities. His goal was simple and radical: to offer light, air, and a view of the sea to functional architecture stripped of historical ornament.

The complex was completed in 1934. The apartments are staggered so that the façades do not block one another, while the rounded corners and pale surfaces evoke modern ocean liners. Nearby, the beach watchtowers, changing rooms, and the former Bellevue Theatre extend the same graphic language.

Jacobsen often designed everything, from the building to the furniture. This overall control explains the coherence of the area, where handles, signage, and proportions all contribute to a shared experience. The project was also a response to the democratization of leisure: the suburban train made it possible for Copenhagen residents to reach the coast quickly.

From Strandvejen, observe the oblique orientation of the wings and the repetition of the balconies. On the beach, the famous blue-and-white towers form small design manifestos. Please respect the privacy of residents, however: Bellavista remains a lived-in residential complex, not an open-air museum.

The excursion combines naturally with Dyrehaven or Ordrupgaard. It shows that Danish modernism was born not in exhibition halls, but in a very concrete reflection on sunlight, housing, and leisure. In fine weather, the architecture looks almost Mediterranean; under a gray sky, its precision becomes even more evident.
en.Musée Ordrupgaard:
A collector’s house, a sinuous extension by Zaha Hadid, and an underground wing by Snøhetta coexist in the Ordrupgaard park. Wilhelm Hansen, a businessman and insurance executive, assembled with his wife Henny an important collection of French and Danish art in the early 20th century. Their villa, completed in 1918, was conceived as both a home and a showcase.

The collection brings together Corot, Courbet, Degas, Gauguin, Monet, Pissarro, and Renoir, alongside painters from the Danish Golden Age. Hansen bought quickly and ambitiously, but a financial crisis forced him in 1922 to sell part of the works. He then rebuilt the collection, a testament to a passion more enduring than his fortune.

In 2005, Zaha Hadid’s extension introduced dark, fluid volumes that follow the slope of the site. Snøhetta’s addition, opened in 2021, sinks beneath the landscape to provide new galleries without overpowering the villa. The dialogue between the architectures alone is worth the visit.

In the garden is also Finn Juhl’s house, preserved with its furnishings. Built in 1942, it shows how the architect arranged colors, artworks, and circulation. Notice how each seat is placed in relation to a window or a painting: design becomes a domestic choreography.

Ordrupgaard calls for a leisurely visit. Alternate between historic rooms, contemporary spaces, and a walk among the park’s installations. Opening hours may vary between exhibitions, and booking is advisable on very busy days. The site brings together painting, architecture, and design without reducing any of these fields to mere decor.
en.Louisiana Museum of Modern Art:
Few museums create such a gentle transition between an art gallery, a lawn, and the Swedish horizon. Louisiana opened in 1958 in a 19th-century villa acquired by Knud W. Jensen. The name was already there: the first owner had named the house after his three wives, all named Louise.

Architects Vilhelm Wohlert and Jørgen Bo designed low wings connected by glass galleries. Rather than imposing an isolated monument, they let the architecture follow the terrain, the trees, and the views across the Øresund. Later extensions have preserved this principle, giving the impression of a museum that grew almost naturally over the decades.

The collection and exhibitions cover international modern and contemporary art. Giacometti, Moore, Warhol, Kusama, and Bourgeois appear alongside Nordic artists. The Giacometti Room, overlooking a pond, is famous for the harmony between slender sculptures, light, and landscape.

The sculpture park is not just an extra for good weather. The works change depending on the visitor’s position, the seasons, and the movement of boats in the distance. Look for Henry Moore’s sculptures on the slopes, then walk down toward the shore; the museum shapes the gaze as much through its windows as through its walls.

Located in Humlebæk, Louisiana is about forty kilometers from Copenhagen and can be reached by train. Half a day is a reasonable minimum. Temporary exhibitions draw large crowds, but the outer galleries and the park always offer a calmer pace.
en.Château de Frederiksborg:
Frederiksborg seems to float on three islets in the middle of Hillerød Lake. Christian IV had the castle rebuilt between 1602 and 1620 in a spectacular Dutch Renaissance style. Red brick, pale sandstone, gables, and spires formed a statement of power meant to rival the great courts of Europe.

The castle served for coronations and for ceremonies of the Order of the Elephant. The richly decorated chapel largely escaped the great fire of 1859, which destroyed much of the interior. The brewer J. C. Jacobsen, founder of Carlsberg, then financed the restoration and helped create the Museum of National History, opened in 1878.

The rooms display portraits, furniture, and objects tracing several centuries of Danish history. It is not only about admiring kings: clothing, battle scenes, and depictions of scholars reveal the way the nation has built its memories. Contemporary portraits extend this gallery into our own time.

In the courtyard, look up at the countless sculpted details and the Neptune Fountain. Then cross over to the restored Baroque garden, laid out in terraces and plant monograms. From the central axis, the castle appears as a carefully framed backdrop of water and flower beds.

Hillerød is less than forty kilometers from the capital. The train makes the excursion easy, but you should allow time for the rooms and the gardens. Frederiksborg is the perfect complement to Rosenborg: one feels like an intimate royal cabinet, the other like a vast stage for dynastic display.
en.Château de Kronborg:
In Helsingør, Kronborg commands the narrowest passage of the Øresund, where Sweden seems almost within earshot. In the 15th century, King Erik of Pomerania established a fortress here to control the Sound Dues, a tax paid for centuries by ships entering or leaving the Baltic.

Frederik II transformed the fortress into a Renaissance palace between 1574 and 1585. After a fire in 1629, Christian IV had the decorations restored. The bastions, casemates, and cannons, however, recall that the site remained a major military stronghold. The Swedes occupied it in 1658 and carried off part of its treasures.

Kronborg is world-famous for its association with Hamlet, although Shakespeare probably never visited Denmark. The name Elsinore, the English version of Helsingør, was enough to evoke a strategic and ominous Nordic court. Theatrical performances have sustained this connection since the 19th century.

Descend into the casemates to meet the statue of Holger Danske. According to legend, this hero sleeps beneath the castle and will awaken if Denmark is threatened. In the courtyard, compare the refinement of the Renaissance façades with the stark strength of the ramparts facing the sea.

Added to the World Heritage list in 2000, Kronborg lies about forty-five kilometers from Copenhagen. The train ride follows the coast and makes it possible to combine the visit with Helsingør’s old town or the maritime museum housed in a former dry dock.
en.Cathédrale de Roskilde:
The two spires of Roskilde dominate a city that was one of the earliest political and religious centers of the Danish kingdom. The present cathedral, begun around 1170, is among the first major Gothic brick buildings in Northern Europe. This material, less costly than stone, made it possible to create an ambitious architecture suited to local resources.

Since the 15th century, most Danish sovereigns have been buried here. The funeral chapels added over time form an astonishing catalogue of styles: Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, Neoclassicism, and contemporary creations. Each dynasty wanted to leave its own mark around the medieval nave.

The cathedral has been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995. It does more than simply line up sarcophagi; inscriptions, frescoes, and monuments tell the story of Denmark's European alliances. The presence of powerful queens, especially Margrete I, is a reminder that monarchical history is not limited to warrior kings.

Look for the column on which the supposed heights of several sovereigns are engraved, then observe how the chapels open out like side rooms. Outside, the color of the bricks changes with the light and reveals successive restorations. The current spires date from the 17th century.

Roskilde is about thirty kilometers from Copenhagen. The cathedral and the Viking Ship Museum make for a complete excursion, linking Christianization, monarchy, and maritime memory. Be sure to check the services, as the monument remains a living church.
en.Musée des navires vikings de Roskilde:
Five black ship silhouettes rest facing Roskilde Fjord like skeletons put back in order. They were deliberately sunk around 1070 in the Skuldelev channel to block access to the town. Recovered and then excavated between 1957 and 1962, they represent different functions: warfare, coastal trade, long-distance transport, and fishing.

The museum opened in 1969 around these remains. The original fragments are held in place by discreet structures that make it possible to understand the forms without inventing the missing parts. Wood analyses have revealed varied origins, from Norway to Ireland, proof of maritime networks far broader than the Viking raider stereotype.

In the shipyard, shipwrights and researchers build replicas using tools and experimental techniques. The warship Havhingsten fra Glendalough even sailed to Dublin, testing speed, maneuverability, and life conditions on board. Archaeology here becomes a physical practice, subject to wind and waves.

Observe the difference between the long, narrow hull of a warship and the broader belly of a cargo vessel. The rivets, clinker-built joints, and tool marks provide clues about the builders’ collective labor. In season, boat trips make it possible to feel directly how these shapes behave on the water.

The museum is a perfect complement to the nearby cathedral. On one side, the royal tombs of a Christian kingdom; on the other, the ships of a mobile society in the midst of transformation. Together, they show that the Viking Age was neither isolated nor abruptly erased.
en.Frilandsmuseet — musée en plein air:
Farms, mills, workshops, and island houses have been dismantled and then reassembled in a vast landscape near Lyngby. Founded in 1897, Frilandsmuseet is among the oldest open-air museums in the world. Its goal was to save rural architecture threatened by industrialization and changes in agriculture.

The buildings come from Denmark, the Faroe Islands, and former Danish territories. They are not arranged at random: gardens, fences, fields, and paths recreate their original environment as closely as possible. Regional differences appear in thatched roofs, timber framing, stonework, and the layout of the farmyards.

Farm animals, craft demonstrations, and seasonal activities add a tangible dimension to the visit. The smoke from a hearth, the sound of a mill, or the small size of a room correct the overly polished images found in books. Rural daily life becomes an experience of scale, smell, and temperature.

Step inside several farms and compare the space given to people, livestock, and storage. Look for windbreaks, the orientation of the buildings, and signs of social status. A seemingly simple house may reveal a highly sophisticated organization of resources.

The grounds are immense; comfortable shoes and several hours are needed. Admission is generally free, but some activities follow a schedule. Frilandsmuseet offers a green retreat and a lively introduction to a Denmark that the palaces of the capital rarely convey.
en.ARKEN Museum for Samtidskunst:
A shipwreck-like building rises behind the dunes of Ishøj. ARKEN opened in 1996, designed by the young architect Søren Robert Lund. The oblique axes, concrete walls, and long central gallery create a deliberately dramatic architecture, devoted to international contemporary art.

The museum is part of the cultural transformation of the southwest suburbs of Copenhagen. Rather than concentrating all the major institutions in the center, the project combined coastal landscape, new infrastructure, and access to art. The collection includes, in particular, an important body of works by Damien Hirst as well as contemporary Nordic art.

The surrounding park was redesigned to bring the water closer to the museum and restore a lagoon landscape. Sculptures, walkways, and vegetation extend the exhibitions outdoors. The building is therefore no longer just an isolated hull: it functions as a cultural harbor between beach, embankments, and residential districts.

In the main gallery, observe how the slanted walls disrupt perspectives. Some works seem to struggle against the architecture, while others use it as a backdrop. Outside, look for reflections of the structure in the canals and for the way the volumes change as you approach from the station.

ARKEN is located about twenty kilometers from the center and can be combined with a walk on Ishøj Beach. Temporary exhibitions strongly shape the experience; check the program before you go. The site reveals a metropolitan capital extending its art scene far beyond its historic walls.
en.CopenHill — Amager Bakke:
Skiers descend the roof of a plant that turns waste into heat and electricity. CopenHill, built on Amager Bakke, opened to the public in 2019. The firm BIG imagined an artificial slope, trails, and a climbing wall above a massive industrial facility, overturning the idea that infrastructure must be hidden.

The plant processes the region’s non-recyclable waste and feeds the district heating network. Its environmental role must be understood with nuance: incineration produces energy and limits landfill use, but it emits carbon and does not replace waste reduction. The building thus gives concrete form to the compromises of urban transition.

The façade is made up of large stacked metal modules. A chimney was originally meant to emit rings of steam symbolizing each tonne of CO₂, a spectacular idea that did not become part of daily operation. Even so, the project retains a strong educational dimension thanks to views of the installations and the harbor.

Take the elevator or the outdoor paths to see Copenhagen from an unusual angle. Wind turbines, canals, downtown towers, and the Øresund Bridge appear in a single panorama. The green slope surface changes texture with the weather; it does not exactly mimic snow, but it makes year-round use possible.

CopenHill is located near Refshaleøen and can be combined with a visit to Copenhagen Contemporary. The sports activities are fee-based, while access to the trails may be subject to specific conditions. Even without skiing, the site is worthwhile for its architecture and for the debate it opens about the visibility of our waste.
en.Centre historique de Køge:
Kirkestræde lines some of the oldest surviving half-timbered houses in Denmark. Køge was founded as a market town in the late 13th century, near the mouth of the river. Its large regular square, its harbor, and its old streets bear witness to a prosperity built on trade between Zealand, the Baltic, and the surrounding countryside.

The town has a remarkable ensemble of 16th- and 17th-century houses. The exposed beams, jettied upper stories, and back courtyards show how commerce, storage, and living space were interwoven. Restorations have preserved irregularities that overly perfect reconstructions would have erased.

Køge is also linked to the witch trials known as the Køge Huskors, between 1608 and 1615. Accusations of possession and magic led to several executions. The local museum places these events in the religious and social tensions of the time rather than turning them into a simple dark legend.

On the square, notice the generous scale of the market and its relationship to Saint Nicholas Church, whose tower also served as a maritime landmark. In Kirkestræde, look for the carved dates and the differences in infill between the timber frames. Each facade is a small document about the materials available and the status of its inhabitants.

Køge is located about forty kilometers south of Copenhagen and can be reached by train. The town is compact enough for a few hours’ walk, but the modern harbor and the KØS Museum of Art can extend the visit. It is a less crowded alternative to Roskilde or Helsingør.

de.Château de Rosenborg et Jardin du Roi:
Rosenborg scheint im Jardin du Roi wie eine Zierkiste aus Ziegeln zu stehen, gespickt mit Türmen und Giebeln. Christian IV. ließ diese Lustresidenz ab 1606 außerhalb der damaligen Stadtmauern errichten. Bis 1633 schritt der Ausbau in Etappen voran; das Schloss folgt dem niederländischen Renaissance-Stil, den der Herrscher besonders schätzte, mit rotem Backstein, hellem Sandstein und Kupferdächern.

Der König suchte nicht nur nach einer schönen Kulisse. Rosenborg bot einen intimeren Zufluchtsort als die großen offiziellen Paläste und öffnete sich zu einem Garten, der für Muße, Obst und Blumen angelegt war. Christian IV. starb hier 1648. Später nutzten die Herrscher die Residenz seltener, was paradoxerweise dazu beitrug, alte Innenräume und Objekte zu bewahren.

Seit dem 19. Jahrhundert beherbergt das Schloss die königlichen Sammlungen. Im Untergeschoss befinden sich die Kronjuwelen und die Insignien, darunter die Kronen des Absolutismus. Drei lebensgroße silberne Löwen bewachen den Thron; sie erscheinen noch heute bei castra doloris, den Trauerzeremonien für Monarchen. Ihr spektakulärer Glanz steht im Kontrast zu den engen Räumen des Hauses.

Der Lange Saal, 1624 vollendet, besitzt eine reich verzierte Decke und Wandteppiche, die die Siege Christians V. im Schonenkrieg schildern. Jeder Raum funktioniert wie eine Herrschaftskapsel: Porträts, Kabinette, Waffen und Möbel zeigen, wie die Monarchie ihr Bild lange vor den modernen Medien formte.

Draußen bemerken Sie die eisernen Anker, die die Backsteinmauern verstärken und an den Fassaden Muster zeichnen.
